## The Initiative

Initiative 86, also known as the Prohibiting Force-Feeding of Birds Act of 2026, would prohibit force-feeding practices and ban the sale or distribution of any product resulting from force-feeding a bird, including foie gras.

## Campaign and Support

Pro-Animal DC submitted more than 46,000 signatures from D.C. voters—nearly twice the minimum required to qualify for the ballot. With early voting starting, D.C. residents will decide whether to ban the luxury liver from city menus and markets.

At-large D.C. Council candidate Oye Owolewa joined activists to hand out stickers and yard signs proclaiming, "Save the ducks, vote yes on I-86." The campaign has attracted unlikely allies, including DC Carnivores meat-fluencer James Nance and local chain Busboys and Poets, which has endorsed Initiative 86.

## Opposition Campaign

Butterworth's chef Bart Hutchins has been one of the most vocal opponents of the initiative and recently wrote an op-ed in the Washington Post about why he's proud to serve foie gras. Hutchins defended the practice, arguing that while force feeding looks terrible, the duck's esophagus is "desensitized" and that ducks in the wild gorge themselves before migration, with foie gras farming amplifying a natural biological process.

## Enforcement and Timeline

If passed, the ban would take effect July 1, 2027, with fines of $1,000 to $5,000 per violation—and additional penalties for each day a violation continues.

Measure 309, launched by Pro-Animal Future, would prohibit the construction and operation of slaughterhouses within the city, including shutting down the largest industrial lamb slaughterhouse in the country.

## Future Plans

The group prefers to run measures in even year elections, and it's going to expand slowly, looking at a few cities next election cycle, and then getting to many more cities after that, and hopefully getting maybe to a statewide campaign. Goals include building a strong grassroots campaigning organization in one city from which we can spread to other cities and eventually pursue a statewide campaign.
